 Expect something new weekly.

articles.title: Pseudo-Rewards
articles.subtitle: "I deserve this" isn't going to cut it anymore. Here's what will.
articles.description: "I deserve this" isn't going to cut it anymore. Here's what will.
articles.content:
I held myself to a fairly strict standard throughout June. I ate no junk food. I walked 10k steps every day. I ran 4 days a week, and lifted weights the other 3. I read for 30 minutes every day.

I’m awesome, right?

Well, not so fast. Yesterday I ate a whole pizza. Not like a personal pizza. A multiple-person, large pizza. I mean, I made it through the month, right? Aren’t I supposed to reward myself?

Rewards

Before digging into my pizza mania, I want to address a certain line of thinking I’ve noticed in one of the newer therapeutic flavors of personal development that seems to denounce the idea of earned rewards. The dialogue goes something like this:

“Why are you rewarding hard work?”

“Does that mean you don’t deserve a reward if you don’t do something hard first?”

“What do you believe about yourself that means you don’t deserve good things inherently?”

Everything, then, has to stem from feelings of insufficiency and shame. What if, however, I simply want to train my animal brain to enjoy doing things that are hard for me to do? Does it have to come back to how I feel about myself and the events of my early childhood?

Now we have that out of the way. I am not throwing away the concept of rewards as a whole, because it seems they can be very helpful. But it needs some adjustment.

Pizza Pizza

So I eat this whole pizza. In my head, leading up to it, there are a few thoughts going through my head:

  1. There aren’t any rules about junk food, so I’m totally good to go on this one.

  2. This is not going to feel good.

  3. This is a reward, right? Totally fine to feel shitty after. I’m rewarding myself.

Here’s the most interesting piece. This ordering was the order that my brain put them in. The real conflict was between 1) & 2). 3) was just the tiebreaker brought in to make me feel better about leaning toward 1).

I made a point to not throw away the entire idea of a reward–but this was no reward. This was something dark, a desire to let go of structure and sink back into something comfortable, masquerading as a reward.

Pseudo-Rewards

This seems to be the prevailing mistake that most people make when thinking about rewards. You’ve probably heard it before (maybe even from yourself):

“I’ve been good; I deserve this cookie.”

“I got up early today, so I bought myself lunch.”

“I’ve worked out every day; I deserve a rest.”

These are not rewards. These are back-rationalized decisions. I wanted a cookie, and then the only way I could rationalize eating it was naming all of the ways I’ve been “good”. I really want to go out to lunch, and then I remembered that I got up early, and hence deserve a reward. I’m tired and don’t want to work out, and remembering that I’ve worked out a lot made me feel good enough to take a rest day.

This is where I agree with the therapeutic self-helpers. If you’re doing the thing simply because you want to, tricking yourself into believing it was for some other reason doesn’t help you. Just have it if you’re going to have it. No smoke and mirrors needed.

But. As I said–these are not rewards. These are independent decisions, with their own agendas, masquerading as rewards.

Bonus: Creating Real Rewards

So let’s try. Let’s actually find out how rewards can work for us. We know from countless studies that mammals will exhibit strange behaviors when they are rewarded in certain ways (do your own study and visit a casino). That doesn’t seem to be the case in my situation; I don’t feel any more desire to go do another disciplined monthlong challenge than before I ate that pizza.

Rewards work best when they are:

  1. Not the main motivator. We want the reward to work as a hint for your brain that says hey, strengthen that neural connection; it led me to something good. Find your own motivation for doing the thing, and let the reward be the cherry on top that greases the neural pathways.

  2. Random. This is the one that drives us crazy. Giving random rewards really solidifies the behavior.

  3. Repeated. Make the rewards small enough that your brain can learn to desire the small behaviors that lead to those rewards. Giving yourself one reward at the end of a month of hard work creates a hard problem for your brain to solve: “Wait, which piece got us this thing?”

Here’s an example of a fairly complex reward system I’m experimenting with. It hits the 3 requirements, but may be more complicated than necessary for you.

If you are sold on the idea and want to try something simpler, pick 3 rewards of varying degrees–mobile game, scrolling, a “cheat” snack, etc. Choose a behavior that you want to reinforce (make it significantly large / small to fit the reward size). Make sure you have a real reason to want to reinforce it. Anytime you complete it, roll a die and let that decide your reward–something like 1 or 2 for a small reward, 3 or 4 for nothing, 5 for a medium, and 6 for a large.

Have fun.

articles.title: Running Away From Stress
articles.subtitle: Rumination's fundamental message that I'm missing.
articles.description: Rumination's fundamental message that I'm missing.
articles.content:
“I’m feeling stressed.” I think to myself.

“No, you’re not.” My future self retorts, unheard because of the limits of space-time.

It’s true. I wasn’t feeling stressed. Stress was coming for me, but I was doing everything in my power to run away and throw whatever I could (planning, busyness, rationalization) in its way.

It would have been more truthful if I had instead thought:

“I’m not feeling stressed, but I should be.”

Last night I was lying in bed, ruminating. There were a number of key concerns that kept popping into my mind: many related to business, a tenant, and other random to-dos that I really didn’t want to forget.

Each time something new popped up, I would feel a slight twinge of panic that would quickly get shut down with some good old-fashioned planning.

“I don’t need to feel that, and here’s the logic to support why not.”

Finally, something pushed me over the edge. I couldn’t run from it any longer, and I felt the full rush of stress, panic, anxiety, whatever you want to call it. And then, I went right to sleep, finally at peace.

It is my inclination that the ‘problem’ of rumination is not solved by thinking more. It’s not because I worry too much. It seems to be the opposite: I don’t worry enough (and by worry, I mean accepting and not pushing away the emotion we’re talking about).

Rumination isn’t a problem of the thinking mind. It is a repeated attempt to use my thinking mind to solve a problem that has nothing to do with it. The ‘fix’ isn’t to stop thinking. The ‘fix’ is to confront the problem where it lies.

In my example, it seemed as if my body simply wanted me to feel this certain emotion. The more and more I pushed it away, thinking “oh, I’m stressed, this sucks,” the more my emotional brain went “Just feel it one fucking time, and then you won’t be!”

Take a second to imagine the hopeless frustration of an entity incapable of communicating but through emotion, whose one job is to relay a message to a separate entity who is completely disinterested in listening to emotion.

It’s like having a deaf child and refusing to learn ASL, all while failing to even recognize that they are not capable of using the type of communication we are familiar with.

So that’s where I was, my emotional brain getting more and more frustrated and my rational brain failing to see the sole message it was trying to get through to me. It wasn’t until my rational brain was overwhelmed that the message got through, which begs the question:

What if I had listened earlier?

articles.title: Willpower Assets
articles.subtitle: Wont and Wellbeing
articles.description: Wont and Wellbeing
articles.content:
Most days lately, I’ve been running out of steam around midday. My energy (and motivation) comes in hot after my first cup of coffee. From there, it’s an uphill battle to get back. It’s not just energy either; it’s attitude. On days when I feel drained, I also feel less capable, less ready to take on the world and any of its problems that dare face me.

When I think about willpower (my overall ability to do what I set out to do), there are two easy pieces that I think get overlooked. The first is physical well-being; the second is behavioral wont.

At a given moment, I may feel as though I “can’t do it” and need a rest. Or I may feel like I’m on top of the world, ready to blast through the next wall I see. In the prior situation, it feels impossible to do the simplest things: even sitting at my computer and checking my to-do list. In the latter, it feels easy and enjoyable.​

Most of us associate “willpower” with the first (and that’s the kind of willpower I’ve been trying to exert recently). What if a more effective strategy was not to fight through the type of momentary impedance as the initial scenario placed in front of us, but instead to focus on changing to the second state?

Rather than “How can I get through this?” the question becomes “How can this be easy?” or “How can I enjoy this?” This puts us in a different frame, arguably a better one with a longer time horizon. Fighting it, in the best case, results in a momentary burst of energy. Switching states results in that, plus more.

That’s why I am thinking of the elements of my “state” as an asset, a regularly paying off feature of where I’m at in life. Fighting through low energy is like working a manual labor job; improving my state to make it easier is like buying a machine to handle the work for me. It’s an investment, but it pays off the more I get to use it.

Willpower assets come in 2 forms, as I mentioned above: behavioral wont and physical well-being. These are the 2 ways we make decision-making easier. Having either one pays off over the duration that it is maintained.

Behavioral Wont

Behavioral wont is the set of things we are used to, or what feels normal and expected. If I think that running is a crazy activity and I rarely see anyone else do it, I won’t naturally think it’s a good decision to do it. Monkey see monkey more-likely-to do.

When people get into running, they’re far more likely to get into it if they join a run club. They see others doing it, and it becomes extremely normal to run. That tips the scales heavily in their decision-making process.

It isn’t just other people; it’s also about what we make normal. If you are comfortable writing every day, because it’s something you’ve done for years, the decision to write will happen quickly and without thought. For someone who wants to write but never has, writing is not contained in their wont, and they will likely struggle.

Behavioral wont is built over time. The mistake many of us make is expecting that our brain’s understanding of what is normal can shift instantaneously simply because we want it to. It doesn’t work this way. Updating behavioral wont is a very doable process, but it requires time for the brain to reset to the new normal. Transitioning slowly and consistently is the upfront cost that will pay off handsomely once you are the owner of this type of asset.​

Physical Wellbeing

If behavioral wont tips the scales naturally, physical wellbeing puts my hand on the scale.

Do you ever notice how your eating patterns change when you haven’t slept well? I’ve noticed it myself. I crave food differently when my body is not in its 100% state.

When I don’t workout, I’m typically in a worse mood, and less likely to do something about it. If I eat poorly, I have less energy.

All of these things tie into this idea: We are able to make the best long-term decisions when our momentary health is optimized. This is an asset that pays off immediately. You can sleep well one night and upon waking have about twice the energy that you felt the day before. Go for one run and notice the motivation that you’ll be able to ride for hours after.

Neither of these involves “grit”. Rather, they both make grit feel less, well, “gritty”. When building willpower (the ability to take actions that reflect your values), having some assets that make it easier isn’t such a bad idea.

articles.title: Natural Drives and "Why"'s
articles.subtitle: When pushing past our limits becomes shockingly easy
articles.description: When pushing past our limits becomes shockingly easy
articles.content:
A few days ago, I went for a run with my dog, Reba.

We made it to our halfway point, which meant it was time to turn around. She decided that instead of running back, she was going to sit in place and simply endure the light tugging on her leash and coercing I sent her way.

She’s 50% Siberian Husky. We were in the Texas sun. This was not what she was built for.

As much as I wanted to feel for her and “see her struggle”, I knew we needed to get home. And we were a few miles from there. So I dropped the leash and started running back without her.

I figured “She’ll catch up, and she can run at her own pace.”

We were on a trail that doesn’t cross any roads, so I felt ok about her being off-leash. Plus, she was so tired, there was no way she’d run off. Right?

So we ran like that for some time. She was about 20 paces behind me, and every minute I’d check on her. We stopped off for a dip and drink from the creek, then continued.

When we were about a quarter mile from home, I saw a switch flip in her brain.

Here she was lolly-gagging along, tongue hanging out of the side of her mouth, when something moved in the woods to our left.

Her ears shot up, and her entire demeanor changed in a heartbeat. The dog I had failed to convince to run with me sprinted past me and veered off into the woods, where I saw a fully grown white-tailed deer looking out at us.

My point in telling you this is not to say that you should look for deer if your dog is tired. In fact, quite the opposite, and I learned my lesson with this one.

​

What I can say is that the energy and willingness to exert it changed so drastically in my dog that I almost couldn’t believe it. As she sprinted after that deer, I saw zero hesitation, zero fatigue, not even a second thought about whether her body had the energy.

​And on top of that, she looked like she was having the time of her life.

When I hear things about “pushing past your limits”, I’m often quickly turned off. I imagine a grueling process of pain and discomfort.

This story shows a different option. With the proper fuel (and in my dogs case, one of the most potent and deeply rooted sources of fuel) we are capable of not only pushing ourselves to new places, but also doing it in a way that feels exciting, fun, and natural.

That’s what understanding your “why” is really about. It’s not about forcing a lifestyle upon yourself or trying to create masochism for harder workouts.

It’s finding the things you care about, the things that give you energy naturally, and allowing those to fuel you in the direction you really want to go.

articles.title: Negotiating
articles.subtitle: And why it's not always a bad thing
articles.description: And why it's not always a bad thing
articles.content:
This week I had a really cool guest on the podcast, a man named Chris Harris.

There were a number of shocking and inspiring stories he told me from his life: watching his mom get arrested, being homeless as a teenager, having brain surgery (literally 8 weeks before we recorded this episode), and a number of other crazy occurrences.

Yet, with all of those extremely unique experiences he shared, one seemingly inconsequential thing he said has been sticking with me:

“I don’t negotiate with myself.”

This morning, I woke up at 7:30am with an alarm. I was having a good dream (I don’t remember what it was about, but I remember feeling relaxed and excited) when my vibrating watch shook me back to reality.

I knew I was behind on sleep from the day before (early-morning flights will do that), but I had also set out my running clothes and shoes the night before, making it very hard for me to ignore. I thanked and cursed my previous self as I tried to decide what to do.

I was negotiating.

I couldn’t just go back to sleep. That didn’t seem right to just throw out the plan completely. But man, I was not quite ready to go run. So I came to an agreement with myself: I would put on my running clothes, and then on my way out I could sleep on the couch for 30 minutes, if I decided at that point that I still wanted to.

​I got my shorts and running shoes on, and walked out to take my promised nap…

To find Reba (my dog) sitting smack dab in the center of the couch. She looked up at me as if to say: Good luck getting me up, I didn’t make any plans to run this morning.​

I ended up taking a short nap on the chair next to her, and though it took some convincing for her, we ended up doing the run 30 minutes late, at 8 am.

I’m now writing this an hour later, and I feel pretty good about that. Would I have been better off if I said “No negotiating” and went right out at 7:30? It’s quite possible. The Chris Harris method may be the optimal one.​

It also may not be what most of us need to hear.

I want us to imagine now that there are two parts of each of us. It’s a simplification that, I think, works here.

One part wants comfort. It wants to relax, it wants to feel good right now.

The other part wants to achieve. It wants to make progress, and it wants to move forward.

For a lot of people, these two parts are in constant tension. Then, there are those who “don’t negotiate”. In other words, one of these parts has taken control, and there is no longer a dialogue between them when it comes to decision making.

In Chris’ case, that seems to be a good thing. He goes to the gym without a second thought (even after brain surgery, which stopped him from actually working out, he still went to the gym). He doesn’t negotiate.

For every case like his, there are a thousand people who also don’t negotiate. Those are the people in whom the comfort part has begun to make the calls. They could say the exact same thing that he does: “I don’t negotiate. I don’t even consider going to the gym.”

The problem isn’t negotiating. The problem is not giving power to the part that we want to be better at negotiating.

articles.title: Success
articles.subtitle: Happiness is just a decision (and some time) away
articles.description: Happiness is just a decision (and some time) away
articles.content:
I often hear podcast interviews in which someone prefaces a story about themselves with something like, “Some people would see my life as successful.” Sometimes it’s more tongue-in-cheek, when a very accomplished person says something like “I’ve done a few things that weren’t completely stupid”.

It is a completely understandable display of humility, but beneath it lies something more interesting. It seems almost as if they are saying “I’ve done the things that make me successful, but I don’t really know whether I actually am successful”.

In this humble brag, they’re actually revealing that there may be confusion about what they have done. And that’s why today, I want to talk about success.

Ten Months

I have spent 10 months working on something that has netted me $0. In fact, it has netted me less if you count the money I have put into it, and much less if you count the time.

For some reason, it still feels like just a few. When I realize how long it has been, I feel it. I feel like I’ve made a mistake, like I’ve been unsuccessful. After all, what is success but a monetary value?

Then I return to reality. I recognize the truth of the situation. I have spent ten months of my life working on a project that I want to be working on, that I literally built from scratch.

In this frame, the $0 income is more of an inconvenience than a dealbreaker. I should probably figure that part out, but it sure as hell doesn’t mean I haven’t been successful.​

Defining success

Rather than going in this roundabout way where it takes 10 months to define what success means–my claim today is that deciding what success means when beginning a pursuit is a way to get much more fulfillment out of the act of pursuing. It protects against future ‘oh shit it’s been 10 months’ moments, because it maintains awareness throughout.

Consider what you are spending your time on. Pick something that is taking significant time (or that you wish to begin spending more time on), and do two things:​

  1. Determine how most people would measure your success in this pursuit. If you are wanting to go to the gym more, the external measure may be how impressed your coworkers are as your body adapts.

  2. Determine how you would like to define success. You might want to feel healthier, to have more energy, or be more athletic. You might even just want to impress your coworkers.

Importantly, these can be the same thing. I am not telling you not to use external motivators or not to listen to the outside world. However, I am saying that listening to the external world is a choice, and it’s yours (and mine) to make.

​There are still constraints in this world. Money is a necessary component of survival, as is health. You have to respect those as pieces of reality. But when it comes to deciding what it is that I am optimizing for, what it would mean for me to be successful, that is completely up to me.

articles.title: Breaking Cycles
articles.subtitle: Where biology and physiology play bigger roles than I've realized
articles.description: Where biology and physiology play bigger roles than I've realized
articles.content:
Cycles are a common theme in behavior and well-being. We’ve discussed positive and negative feedback loops and how each of those can create behavior cycles. Specifically sticky are the positive ones, that ramp up (or down) until we are really stuck in a behavior.

The feedback loop I’ve found myself in lately is one of poor sleep. Not sleeping too little, but getting poor quality sleep. That happens for a multitude of reasons, but I think I have picked out the biggest one, and it’s perfect for this topic: mistimed sleep due to caffeine consumption.

In other words, my sleep time has been getting pushed back, which leads to less-than-ideal sleep, which leads to more desire for caffeine, which leads to my sleep time getting pushed back, and on and on.

Today, I’m going to explore ideas around breaking this cycle that I am likely to follow and with extrapolation potential (I could just say “quit caffeine tomorrow and go to bed at 10pm”, but that wouldn’t be that helpful to anyone else).

Bedtime

There is clear data, by now, showing that timing of sleep matters for health, on the same level of importance as duration of sleep. It has been shown that large variations in bedtime correlate with higher BMI, fat mass, and insulin resistance. Three things that, generally speaking, correspond to poor health and feeling less than optimal.​

This problem, then, is of utmost importance. Every day that I am not asleep by the same time as the night before is building on this problem–and making me more likely to continue building on it in future days.

Why patterns exists

I am tempted first to look into why these cycles even happen in the first place, and to see if there’s any way that the cycle can be cleanly broken without too much difficulty.​

With negative cycles (not to be confused with negative feedback, as these are positive feedback loops we are discussing), I am often being pushed into a reactive state. Not only is that happening, it is the primary reason I end up in the cycle. Rather than making decisions, I am reacting to what is happening.​

For example, I may decide today to stop drinking so much caffeine. Tomorrow, however, if I wake up a tired wretch, I may just say forget it and run to the coffee machine. I am reacting immediately to the circumstances, in an attempt to feel better.

So two things are happening.

  1. I want to feel better.

  2. I am in a reactive state.

These two work in tandem to provide a foundation for disaster. Wanting to feel better is not a bad or unnatural state in the slightest: it only becomes a problem when all other considerations are thrown away at the behest of my next gratification.

In other words, reaction places too much emphasis on fixing the current problem at hand.

Breaking the cycle

So we have a bit more understanding now. First, that sleep regularity is actually really important to be healthy and happy (and to continue sleeping regularly). Second, being in a reactive state keeps us in cycles.

I want to offer one of the simplest and (maybe) most interesting ideas I’ve stumbled upon recently. It’s based in commonly known practices, but the understanding is based on a connection that I had never recognized before now.​

The magic answer is… taking a few deep breaths.

Ok, ok. That’s not an exciting answer, nor does it feel worthy of your time to have read to this point. Hang in there.

Biology and Me

The connection I’ve been seeing more and more is between my subjective state and my physiological state. It also comes with a breakdown of what we commonly think of as the “self”.

Recently, I was in a group and noticed myself overthinking what I was saying or about to say, which led me to withhold my social contributions. By many definitions, it was social anxiety.

In the state of shut down, I remembered a recent conversation in which a friend of mine had brought to my attention the idea of “fight-or-flight”, and how many of us live our lives in this (reactive) state. On a whim (and because I wasn’t doing anything else, sitting there silently), I tried taking a few deep breaths, really focusing on relaxing. As if my magic, the thoughts and emotions that were holding me back simply stopped popping up, and I was able to rejoin naturally and without fear.​

The profound part of this all is the way in which these thoughts and feelings went away. I think many of us assume that overcoming something will require a fight in which we defeat the debilitating thoughts one by one. Stepping out of this is recognizing that there is no “defeating” these thoughts, at least not in the way we think. These thoughts don’t live by the laws of logic; they can’t be debated. It is in recognizing that they are coming from a source that has been shaken so dramatically that it is spewing fearful and (often) incorrect ideas because it is trying to understand why it feels this level of danger. The correct response is to bring the system back to a place of safety, rather than fight the thoughts and emotions.​

An animal that is in danger will highly prioritize an action that brings relief as soon as possible. It makes sense to do that. The problem is that 99% of the time, I am not facing real danger. My biology is misdiagnosing my surroundings.

Bringing it in

The way to break a cycle is to bring oneself out of a reactive state. The way to move out of a reactive state is to restore the body to a state of relaxation and safety.

Let’s walk through this with my first example.​

  1. I go to sleep late, because I’m not that tired when I usually go to bed.

  2. I wake up, and I don’t feel great. I recognize that coffee will make me feel slightly better, right now. I don’t (yet) consider whether it will continue this negative cycle.

  3. I stop myself for a second. I recognize that I am in a reactive state, which makes short-term rewards seem extremely valuable. I take a second to breathe and notice, and I begin to feel less “on edge”.

  4. I magically begin to see the decision to have coffee differently–not because I consciously made myself think any specific way, but because I have set up my biological system to place less emphasis on feeling better, right now.

  5. I decide whether to have a coffee.

articles.title: Remembering How Things Can Be
articles.subtitle: When it comes, listen
articles.description: When it comes, listen
articles.content:
I’ve been sleeping poorly, eating poorly, and missing exercise. There are reasons I need not go into (not to excuse it or to say that those things weren’t possible for me), but I’ve noticed a drawback in my day-to-day experience as a result.

That comes in the form of less energy, less excitement, and a higher reliance on instant gratification - coffee, food, checking my phone, working distractedly on numerous projects at any one time. Along with that comes a general feeling that things are dull and boring, and will stay that way.

Growing up, I remember feeling this way at times. There’s a certain fear and helplessness that becomes associated with feeling “bad” because of the inability to see beyond it. When I felt anxious, low energy (depressed), or fearful, it seemed inevitable and eternal. That was simply the way it would be: this is how I feel now, forever.

The worst part isn’t the feeling. The worst part is the mental chatter telling me that this is my fault, and that this dull and reliant existence is the way I will be from here on out.

Remembering how things can be

As an adult, I’ve noticed that the fundamental experience I’ve described hasn’t changed. There are still the same stories, the same feelings, and the same impulses.

However, there’s something else, something that is rare and as exciting and beautiful as it is rare. It’s a thought, a reminder, that visits quietly and briefly. It whispers in my ear, “Remember how things have been.” That’s it.

That quiet reminder gives me a chance. It’s an opportunity to see the larger picture that has been obfuscated by the particular fear or apathy that has taken over. It’s not the end, but it could be the beginning.

Listening

As I mentioned, it’s often very quiet and brief. I’ve had the experience of having this blinding beam of optimism in the midst of an episode of stimulation-reliant living, and after not acting on the recognition immediately, I quickly forgot and returned to my ways.

Then there are times when I did act on it, and I built upon the optimism that had been spontaneously generated. That feeling rarely comes on its own, and like a seed, it must be nourished and protected to continue to exist. Listen closely, and take these as the gift they are.

articles.title: The Depth of Sadness
articles.subtitle: A rough take on a challenging emotion, written at 30,000 feet
articles.description: A rough take on a challenging emotion, written at 30,000 feet
articles.content:
Sadness is an emotion I’ve never felt comfortable with, much less accustomed to. It always felt like a fight—either it was something I shouldn’t feel, or at the very least, something I did not want to feel.

Yet it comes, the unstoppable force that forces the yielding of my “immovable” stubbornness to feel it. Sadness is an inevitability of life. It’s scary and uncomfortable. At the same time, there is something comforting about falling into its embrace and feeling into the richness that it brings to experience.

For me, sadness hits like a hole in my lower chest. If I let myself lean into it, it almost feels like I’m falling through my chest into my abdominal space. It’s deep, viscerally deep.

Sometimes when some happening brings upon the sadness, as is the case today, I notice that the feeling in my chest and stomach is not new, like a sore my tongue has just discovered and won’t stop probing. The feeling has been there, and this difficult event has led me to finally explore it.

There’s somewhere to exist peacefully in there. It’s actually not scary, and it’s actually not uncomfortable. Those are only resistances, like my body’s last line of defense before feeling something real. There’s nothing to avoid. It’s an ultimate way to honor life, that we experience the very depth of sadness that loving can cause.

articles.title: The Novelty Drive-Thru
articles.subtitle: "Junk" stimulation's missing component
articles.description: "Junk" stimulation's missing component
articles.content:
My brain is a stimulation-seeking device. It is built to explore, to find the most interesting inputs it can. This is a good thing.

This is the reason that anything gets done. I wouldn’t go back to Jiu Jitsu if I wasn’t hoping to learn something, or complete a submission, or meet someone interesting enough to make it worth it. I wouldn’t write this every week if I didn’t think there was a chance that I would find some new insight that would be profound and exciting to discover.

Our exploration for novelty is a good instinct. However, for most of us, it has been hijacked.

Pathologization

The issue that most of us face with stimulation is akin to the dilemma of processed food. We all have a desire to eat food that works with our bodies’ systems to tell us when we need nourishment. That desire is good, but it isn’t perfect. It can be captured, and has been for many of us. Engineered foods hit our systems in a way that confuses them and makes them believe that it is nourishing in a way that it is not, leading to overeating and malnourishment.

So what’s the solution? To stop eating altogether?

Of course not. We all know this.​

This is the problem we run into with stimulation. We have hundreds of unhealthy sources of stimulation hitting us every single day. The solution, though, is not to denounce stimulation and novelty. This is not a call to join an ashram and spend your days meditating.

Rather, sticking with the food analogy, the guidance follows that we should seek out “healthy” sources of stimulation.

Spotting Unhealthy Stimulation

If you eat a lot of fruit, you will likely not become unhealthier because of it. However, if you flip that and drink a lot of fruit juice, over time, you may find yourself facing increased inflammation, diabetes, or even heart disease. This is not intuitive–it seems that if the fruit is healthy, each of its component parts should be as well. The problem, as we have collectively learned, is that our bodies do not respond the same to each piece in isolation. It’s not about what we are consuming when we drink fruit juice. It’s what we are not.

This sets us up perfectly to understand unhealthy stimulation. It is missing something some key component of healthy stimulation.

Let’s say one day I go out to an event. I’m nervous to go, but I end up meeting a number of cool people. I connect with a few with the intention to keep in contact. It’s exciting. Another day I pull up Instagram and scroll through 20 videos in the span of a few minutes. I feel excited during this as well.

After the event, I feel fulfilled and accomplished. After scrolling IG, I feel… empty.

What was the difference? Both seemed to start with excitement, and then completely diverged from each other. My brain was just doing it’s job of seeking excitement, and in one case was rewarded, in the other heavily penalized. How can it make sense of this?​

The key component that was missed in scenario #2 was what happened at the start of scenario #1: I had to work for the excitement–there was a lead-up, I had to exert energy to get there, and initiate conversation. I had to go through something challenging (nervousness) in order to get the reward. It seems that some type of energy expenditure is a key component of healthy stimulation.

Responsibility

Unfortunately, our brains, for the most part, struggle to understand the unhealthiness of unhealthy stimulation. They’ve come to understand sugar as the “good” part of fruit, and similarly see the dopamine spike as the “good” part of an experience. Because of that, they do not discern between the ones that require work–in fact, they will more likely avoid those (why more people are addicted to social media than to working out).

The onus is on us. I can’t depend on my brain to make the decision, and so I must make it. I don’t keep processed junk food around the house, nor should I keep processed junk stimulation.

What I can’t do is get rid of it completely: I will always be able to access it with a few clicks or taps (the McDonald’s drive-thru of the digital world). But I can control how much it is allowed to infiltrate my life. I can choose the apps on my phone. I can choose which can notify me. I can choose which companies are allowed to email me. I can build routines around how I use the internet. I choose which junk is allowed in my house.

articles.title: Choosing Where You Want To Be
articles.subtitle: What piano can teach us about life and learning
articles.description: What piano can teach us about life and learning
articles.content:
I wish I could tell you how to turn your life into the exact life you want, tomorrow. I wish I could do that for myself, today. I can’t, but I do have some thoughts on the subject.

​Learning something new

I’ve been working on a challenging piano piece (for my ability level) for 6+ months now. Almost every day, I spend a little bit of time practicing the parts that I have already learned and slowly adding on to what I can “get through”–if I’m lucky, I’ll be able to play through one measure (a section of a music piece that in this case represents 4 “beats”) that I couldn’t the day before.

Most measures take me a few days to get the hang of enough to play them directly from the previous measure. The progress is painstakingly slow. I have to fight and claw for each measure, which, when all is said and done, amounts to ~2 seconds of playing time in the final piece. Yet, I find it worth it, and I continue to do it.

Now, I’d like to find what lessons I can take from this extremely slow process that I have followed steadfastly and hopefully apply elsewhere in my life.

The key components

There are a few things that seem to be keeping me going on this piano piece. Those seem to be:

  • The end goal. If there wasn’t something I was working towards (being able to play through an entire piece that I find great), I would never have had the motivation to get started, much less continue at it for this long.

  • Measurable progress. I’m now recognizing that the music term “measure” fits beautifully here. Each measure I learn and can henceforth play is marked off in my mind and brain’s motivation centers. The progress (each measure) brings me one definitive step closer to my end goal.

  • A repeatable habit. My way of continuing progress on a regular basis. For me, that is simply a habit that I now track: “Practice Piano for 10 Minutes”. This ties the progress I see to the action that creates the progress.

If these three components are enough to fuel me in such a slow and challenging pursuit as learning this piano piece, I can’t help but wonder what would happen if I were to apply them elsewhere.​

Music is wonderful as an example because it is so easily portioned off. I can learn a song on an instrument, and clearly check that off. I learned the song measure-by-measure and checked those off as I went. It’s broken down so clearly, in a way that makes motivation much easier.

Other pursuits in life aren’t this kind.

How about working out? Do I want to focus on losing weight and prioritize the number on the scale? Or do I want to prioritize muscle gain, and use the way my muscles look in the mirror? Or my mile time, or any other number of metrics. It becomes harder and much more arbitrary how we select what we define as progress.

Business is the same: do I want to use monetary goals? Or maybe I give more of a shit about the number of people using my product? Or what do people say about it?

Picking what progress means seems pretty hard.​

What I’m realizing as I write this is that each of the above factors only becomes hard when the factor before it is not clearly defined. Here’s what I mean:

I will struggle to choose a repeatable action (habit) that helps in my pursuit if I don’t know what progress means.

I will struggle to define what progress means in the pursuit if I don’t have a clear end goal.

Choosing an end goal, then, becomes the part that’s actually challenging, as the others will naturally flow from it.

That leaves us in a tough spot, which is choosing an end goal. Where do you want to be? That’s a hard question to reckon with, for a few reasons:

  1. There are a lot of “good” end states. I could imagine a number of places I get in life that look pretty good. How do I pick which one to aim for?

  2. The thing I aim for may not make me happy. Lottery winners tell the classic tale of a financial state many of us yearn for, creating drastic unhappiness. It’s not obvious that the states we “want” are what will actually make us happy.

So, I will leave it at that. I could maybe try to think through a way to break through these two and decide on an end goal, but I think I would rather leave that for you to do. What’s an end goal that you haven’t defined? What does progress look like towards that goal? And what action can you repeat that brings you progress?

articles.title: Just Being Tired
articles.subtitle: It's not that bad, try it
articles.description: It's not that bad, try it
articles.content:
It’s now been a few weeks that I’ve been actively working on quitting caffeine. Those weeks have been a roller coaster–I’ve had days on the wagon and days off, but more than half have been “days on”, and that’s a win. I’m getting closer to the point where a morning without coffee can actually be enjoyed (not quite, but I’m getting there).

Last night I did not get optimal sleep (for reference, my Oura sleep score is 75, whereas yesterday it was 91. I can feel the lack of sleep pretty clearly, in grogginess and mental fog. The odd thing? I’m not hating it.

One of the sneaky and sinister harms of a coffee addiction is how it allows for the “covering up” of many feelings, and specifically, the feeling of insufficient sleep. Like Klarna for my biological health, I can push the time when I have to pay the price down the line, so that at least today I don’t have to face it.​

I’ve noticed myself drink far more caffeine on days I don’t sleep well, or even justify staying up late or getting up early with the promise of a cup of coffee to tide over those pesky feelings of fatigue.

When thinking this way, I often end up over-caffeinated and worse off than when I started–now I’m tired AND jittery with the feeling of low blood sugar that too much caffeine can bring.

Interestingly, I’m not sure that the feelings of tiredness were ever the real problem.

I feel tired today, sure. Honestly, though, I wouldn’t say I feel particularly bad. I’d rather feel well-rested, but this isn’t the worst thing.

Yet, I can remember feeling this exact way in the past, and without examining it too much, pouring coffee on the situation. I made the fundamental mistake of assuming feeling different is the same as feeling bad.

In doing this, I created a problem where there wasn’t one. I trained myself to believe that not getting enough sleep would lead to an awful feeling–a feeling that was solvable with coffee.

The tension between how I felt and how I thought I should feel was the problem; it actually had nothing to do with my state itself. That’s what I’m realizing today. I can feel tired, out of it, unfocused, or any other face of sleep deprivation. And that’s okay. I may prefer a different state while at the same time accepting mine for what it is.

It was never the tiredness I hated. What I hated was the desire to feel some way that I couldn’t. It was the tension of not knowing why coffee wasn’t solving the problem that I thought it should. I’m done fighting it (until next time I have coffee).

articles.title: Stories & Stories
articles.subtitle: Letting go, rewriting, building more?
articles.description: Letting go, rewriting, building more?
articles.content:
Let’s talk about stories. Not the stories that we tell around a fire, but the stories that constantly run through our heads, with one speaker and one listener.

Reality is crazy and complex. Understanding it in its totality is impossible, and that is why our brains have evolved to tell stories. The problem is, like analogies, stories always break down at some point and stop describing reality accurately.

​When I make a plan…

I recently made a whole 3-month plan to improve a few areas of my life. Then, about a month and a half in, I injured myself, and the physical goals started to become unrealistic. Once those fell off, the other goals also felt less important, and soon the entire plan had fallen apart.

​Before starting this, there was a story I told myself about creating plans: “When I make a plan, I stick to it.” With this collapse, however, I realized that the story had flipped, drastically: “When I make a plan, it doesn’t happen.”

Without getting too involved in the delicate balance between making plans and taking action, I want to recognize that one event completely flipped a pretty sturdy “story” that had been somewhat controlling the way I lived my life. I didn’t follow through on a plan, so the story that had existed had to be completely thrown out, wholesale. It can’t be true that I follow through on plans if there is even one case in which I don’t.

That left me feeling incapable, like I had lost a piece of control over myself.

Reality

The truth, however, is not that the story was still true despite my one failing (as much as I want that to be the case). The truth is that neither story is true, nor were they ever true. They are stories, slight patterns found in the complexity of life that seemed to hold true, but could never be fully true, for they simply aren’t complex enough to describe reality.

​That is hard to realize. The things we tell ourselves about the world and how we move within it are at best abstractions, and as we saw here, they are often wrong on many levels. Even better, they work in the background, modifying and producing the thoughts and emotions that allow the story to remain true, despite the fact that it can’t be. If I believe that I will simply not follow plans, I will not have the idea to create one, and if I do, it will likely be shut down. I may not even follow one if I do, because of that story itself.

These stories bend reality as we see it into a state that is more understandable. But it isn’t true. It is necessarily missing something.

What to do

So I have brought up what seems to be an insurmountable problem: I don’t want to have these stories controlling how I see and maneuver within the world, but I can’t understand reality without some kind of story to simplify it.​

It doesn’t seem that there is a clear answer. There’s existing advice on this: rewriting stories, letting go of stories that don’t ‘serve you’, or even dropping them all.

The Wisdom Method

My idea is to do what I call the “wisdom method”. Wisdom, as I see it, is the developed understanding of the world and one’s place within it, or the extent to which it is developed. Someone who is wise has developed this, while someone who is not has not. It is accrued through learning and experience, specifically new experience.

The more that we can go through on an experiential level, the more that our brain naturally builds its wisdom, as long as we give it the conditions to do so (proper rest, nutrition, and time to reflect).

The Wisdom Method, then, is the goal of adding complexity to our stories, rather than expecting to throw them away or to rewrite them completely. The truth is, our brains are good at learning. If a story has been written, it is written because it abstracts a certain situation or event in a way that helped you understand it, at that time in your life. The story may not be adaptive (yet), but it was true in that specific instance.

Building on

How does one ‘build’ on a story? First, we challenge them, often. If I don’t think planning works for me, that’s a good sign to try planning something. If I don’t think I can build a successful business, it’s a good sign I should try and see if that is true or not, or put myself into experiences that either disprove, or more likely, build onto the understanding. ‘I can’t follow through on a plan” turns into “I typically don’t follow through on plans when I have too many things going on”. This story still isn’t fully true, but it’s a step closer to reality.

The key here is experience. The brain learns through experience. I can’t simply think through my stories and decide how I want them to be. It doesn’t seem to work, at least not nearly as well. The stories must be lived out.

articles.title: Quitting Again
articles.subtitle: The mind getting hijacked, and taking it back
articles.description: The mind getting hijacked, and taking it back
articles.content:
I’m quitting caffeine (yet again). Or better yet, I’m significantly reducing my caffeine intake. This framing, I’m hoping, will take the edge off of the “never” that scares me, because I do like caffeine oh so much.

Welcome to day 0.

Getting off caffeine, like any regularly used drug, is a process that requires at least a few days to get back to some kind of baseline. There are certainly drugs much harder to get off of, that take more time and / or are more intense in the blast from homeostasis that quitting them entails, but the principle is the same nonetheless.

So I sit here writing, and I can barely think. My mind feels cloudy and slow. Over half of the sentences I’ve written I have already deleted, for they made little sense when I read them back.

Rather than just complain and feel bad for myself, though, I’d like to explain why I’ve decided to quit caffeine this time. As I mentioned, this has happened before. I’ve had a few stretches in the past few years, one lasting 6+ months, in which I drank no caffeine. Let me tell you why I’m putting myself through this again.

I’ve been noticing more and more that caffeine (and coffee, to be precise) has expanded to take up much more of my mental space than I would prefer. When I went on a cruise in January with my lovely girlfriend, my morning coffee was something I looked forward to, even in the evening leading up to it.

When touring apartments recently, the thought “would I enjoy sitting with a cup of coffee here better than the last place” was a serious (if partially unconscious) thought I had regularly.

​It sounds silly, but I think about coffee a whole lot.

At the same time, I greatly enjoy it. I’ve noticed that there is a fear in my mind, something like “If I stop drinking caffeine, will my mornings be enjoyable?” or “What will happen to my work time? Will I be able to motivate myself naturally?” And for some time, I wasn’t sure.

Cue Bryan Johnson. I recently happened to listen to a podcast featuring him. His reminders about the importance of sleep for overall well-being gave me the nudge I needed. I realized at that moment that there was a way for me to enjoy my life just as much, if not more, if I wasn’t drinking coffee. This dependence is not the dependence that I thought it was.

I had been living in this weird state of unconscious behavior, in which I never sat down and looked at the cold, hard, facts.

  1. This habit is becoming negative in how it consumes my mental space.

  2. Quitting may be challenging for a few days.

  3. I will be completely fine and just as happy after those few days.

These three things, as obvious as they sound, had not fully set in until I heard and saw the way that Bryan showed up on the podcast. Here was someone who prioritizes his health and feels great because of it. There’s no need for coffee boosts (so I would assume, I don’t know if he consumes caffeine or not) because everything is working as it should. That’s where I wanted to get to.

With that, I will leave you a few reasons you may want to quit a habit that seems benign or even positive, like my caffeine habit. These go outside of the typical surface-level good / bad categorizations we put on things (like smoking, which is unhealthy, even on the surface).

Why you may want to quit a habit that doesn’t seem “that bad”:

  • It takes over your mind when you aren’t doing it. This was my conundrum, and it seems to be the sign of an addiction. Unless you have a very good reason to keep a habit, I would consider letting it go for this reason alone.

  • It lets you cover up other bad habits. If I sleep poorly, caffeine will make me feel okay, at least temporarily. Scrolling social media (harmless on the surface) may allow you to cover up anxieties or depravations, and keep you from having to feel them. Nicotine, alcohol, etc., can also serve this purpose.

  • You think you need it. As soon as you think you need something, it’s a good sign to dig in. I have definitely felt this way with coffee before, and so I understand how challenging this sounds. Sometimes when the belief is strong, it’s hard to even think about the habit without the mind being wrenched in another direction. As soon as you think you need something, you will be willing to compromise other things to maintain it. That’s a good sign to let it go.

articles.title: The Unconscious Paradox
articles.subtitle: When not answering a question, answers the question
articles.description: When not answering a question, answers the question
articles.content:
When’s the last time someone asked you: “Tell me about a time when you…”?

What did you do? Did you think hard, scanning your memories for one that matched, maybe going through memories in a haphazard and inefficient search method? Maybe you didn’t find anything good, and you had to fit some story into the prompt that was given (like in a job interview).

Lately, I’ve been practicing not coming up with anything when I’m asked questions of this nature.

I first learned this from the Internal Family Systems modality in cognitive behavioral therapy. In this, one is often tasked with labeling parts within their psyche and identifying reactions and responses to prompts and questions by different parts. For example, someone may identify a part of themself that is their 8 year old version. This part may still be scared to speak in front of the class, so they may ask the part, “What are you scared of?”, and then try to understand some kind of response.

My initial thought when learning this was how the fuck do I ask a ‘part’, which is already a pretty loose construct to me, a question, and get its response? I didn’t have a panel of clearly labeled “Will”’s, each with their own specific microphone, in my head.

Each of my first attempts at it was fueled by cognition: rather than asking the part, I would just ask myself, “What would that part of me probably think about this?” I would think through and come up with something.

What I was doing with the IFS technique was akin to asking someone a question, then, as they’re about to answer, speaking loudly over them about what I think they’re going to say.

Upon realizing this, I had a profound experience in which answers just “bubbled” to the surface of my consciousness. Whether or not they were coming from clearing defined “parts” aside, the questions were being answered, and without “me” needing to do anything.

This just goes to show the power of our unconscious mind, and more profoundly, my own lack of awareness of that power.

We assume as though the little piece of the mind that we are aware of, the space in which we witness thoughts, emotions, sensations, and the like, is the one in charge of everything. We pretend as if it is the powerhouse and the executive decision–maker.

We realize how silly that is when it’s said out loud. There are thousands, potentially millions of processes that the brain and nervous system manage at all times, with none of our awareness. Our hearts keep beating. Our blood chemistry adjusts to what we eat and how we move. Our breath comes in and out. All of it is happening completely outside of conscious awareness. Yet my default assumption is always that nothing will get answered if my conscious (and illusory) self is not spearheading the effort to get it answered.

Now, I ask that you try this out. Try asking something of yourself, or if you are brave, wait for the next time you are given a prompt or question. Then consciously hold your consciousness back. Leave your mind open–no effort allowed. You will likely notice at first a void, an emptiness. That’s the right place to be.

Then, watch what comes out of it.

articles.title: The Antidote to Self-Consciousness
articles.subtitle: Why it's seeming partner is the solution to it
articles.description: Why it's seeming partner is the solution to it
articles.content:
I’ve written a few of these about self-consciousness over the past couple of years, but lately the concept has been coming up for me more and more, and I feel as though I have something new to add to my previous picture – due to the “in-my-face” nature of the experience of being self-conscious.

First of all, a definition. In my view, self-consciousness is not simply consciousness of the self, but consciousness of the self as perceived by others in a way that is often catastrophized. For example, a few weeks ago at a men’s group, I blurted out something that, after saying it, I deemed to be stupid and embarrassingly clumsy. I immediately felt the uncomfortable rush of self-consciousness, not because anything changed about my own awareness of myself, but a heightened fear about how the others may now perceive me.

The term “self-consciousness” has broken free of the two individual words that comprise it.

Today, rather than simply talking about what it is, I want to talk about the antidote. The thing that makes self-consciousness impossible, at least momentarily.

If self-consciousness is the perceived (and catastrophized) view of oneself through the lens of another, then the only clear way to break free of it is to collapse the structure you are looking through–rather than looking at yourself through the lens of another, take out the middleman and bring your attention directly upon yourself.

It’s akin to looking at an object in the mirror, then realizing that the object is available to be looked at right in front of you. Better yet, a funhouse mirror in which the object gets distorted and you mistakenly perceive the object incorrectly.​

In moments of self-consciousness, I miss out on the fact that “I” am right here, and rather than trying to see myself through someone else’s perception, I can just look directly at myself. Once that happens, I no longer have the ability to feel self-conscious, because self-consciousness requires that other person’s perception, of which I have robbed my attention.

That is why the antidote to self-consciousness is self-awareness.

The question then becomes “What is self-awareness, and why is it anything different from self-consciousness?” Or better yet, “How do I be self-aware?” Self-awareness is often an overly flaunted virtue that is never actually investigated or fully understood.

My answer to the first question, regarding the difference, is as follows: self-awareness is the understanding of oneself as it is. We are the only ones with true access to the self, and so trying to understand oneself from the point of view of another (as we do when we are self-conscious) is like asking a friend how hungry I am. They may have some idea of the answer (based on my touchiness, or repeated mentions of getting lunch), but the hunger is already directly accessible to me.

The second question is harder to answer, because it requires understanding what the self is, and the reality that it is not at all what we often think it to be. The self as a constant and permanent locus of attention will dissolve as you look closer at it, and the truth becomes a little weirder. The “self” is simply the preexisting rise and fall of objects within the container of consciousness. In other words, self-awareness is no different from mindfulness - being aware of the contents of the mind.

In a moment of self-consciousness, I can immediately become self-aware by simply becoming aware of what is happening in my mind–the flushing of my cheeks, the feeling of increased heart rate, the thought that all attention is on me (and the spiral loop that can feed into). And as soon as I come to this understanding, I am no longer self-conscious. I’m no longer attaching to these contents of consciousness, nor am I trying to understand myself through the convoluted method of using someone else’s eyes. I’m all at once the self and the understanding of it as such.

articles.title: Breaking My Word
articles.subtitle: Even the devil has valid arguments, sometimes
articles.description: Even the devil has valid arguments, sometimes
articles.content:
My girlfriend texted me a few days ago.

“Wanna start a 3-day fast?” (She’s a keeper).

The literal answer to the question was “No, I don’t want to start a fast.” I never really want to start a fast. And usually when I do things like this, I feel the need for some ceremony, a build-up that leads to the moment in which I declare outwardly (into my own psyche) “I AM STARTING A FAST”. There was none of that. This was all too... casual.

I agreed anyway.

The first day went beautifully. My last time doing a fast was at the beginning of the year, when I knocked off 7 days for a personal “record” (it feels dangerous to call it that). Hubris, which I assumed at the time was confidence, was high. Fasting is now easy for me. 3 days is a very short amount of time. I can’t believe how simple this is.

Then, nighttime came. I was around 33 hours into the fast, almost halfway. The cravings started coming on strong. I lay awake for 2 hours, waiting for sleep to rescue me from these unmeetable desires, but it would not. My fasting insomnia was back in full force.

I wanted out. It wasn’t just the hunger, but also the awareness that I was lying awake at a time I normally would be sleeping, something I would pay for tomorrow (which is now today).

And so I ate. Around 1:30 last night, I had a snack and ended up falling asleep about 30 minutes later. My girlfriend would have to continue on her own.

​Rather than self-chastisement (which would be pretty silly here) or feeling bad about/for myself, it’s interesting to reflect on the internal debate that led me to that decision. Let’s break that down.

The first party wanted to stick it out to the end of the fast. Their arguments revolved around self-integrity, following through, and supporting my girlfriend. The opposition used the arguments of sleep, “hangriness” (not ruining otherwise pleasant moments by being hungry during them), and that this wasn’t planned out (and hence, not worth the trouble). The two debaters were my pride (or ego, if you’d rather call it that) and my hunger.

The funny thing is, the sides didn’t give a shit about the things they were arguing; they just cared about getting what they wanted. My hunger didn’t care if I was going to be tired the next day; it simply used whatever it could to convince me that I should eat.

​Where was I in this? It feels like I was in the middle. I had a devil and an angel on my shoulders, except I didn’t know which was which. That begs the question:

How can I make “good” decisions when unknown intentions are involved?

My hunger might have been right in the argument it made about sleep, but the intention of my hunger wasn’t to help me be more rested; it was just to eat. It’s akin to making a deal with a shady businessman: even if the deal seems beneficial, the underlying intentions seem to taint it. At the same time, it might still be the right decision to make. Each argument then had to be taken with a grain of salt in attempt to find the underlying “best” decision.

I almost feel at a loss trying to come up with any realistic solution here. There doesn’t seem to be any good way to go about this without first meditating away all “Sankaras”, a task that I’m not certain is fully possible. It seems that there may be ways to at least get better, if slowly, at making these decisions. As with all pursuits of self-understanding, the path is long and without many signs.​

​So first: meditation. This repeatedly seems to be a good way to understand myself better. Meditation doesn’t need to only happen when I’m sitting with a timer running. It can be when I’m out walking my dog, or writing this, or driving. Anytime I’m doing anything, there is the option to do it with more awareness. A good question to direct inward and spur this meditative state: What is it like being me right now?​

The reason meditation helps with a deeper understanding of the self and the many motivations is that it looks directly at them. While meditating yesterday (before I had crashed and burned on the fast), I realized that the physical feeling of hunger didn’t feel to me like anything that required food to satiate it. Then I noticed that the voice in my head that craved food seemed to be separate from the physical sensation. That was an insight I didn’t have before: the physical craving wasn’t directly causing the craving. The two have become associated, but they are separate. Meditating creates space to understand things like this more clearly.

​Second, reflection. Like I’m doing here. Yours doesn’t have to (and maybe shouldn’t) be public. In either case, spending time with an open mind after the fact seems to be a good thing. For example, I realize today that my hunger side did have a really good argument, and also a really bad argument. I bought both of them.

Taking the time to look back lets me see where I’m understanding myself and my cravings, and where I am being deceived by them. So even though I made a decision that may have been the right one, my reasons for doing so were impure, and can be learned from moving forward.

articles.title: Feeling Better -> Feeling...
articles.subtitle: The loops that keep us in place, and the ones that don't
articles.description: The loops that keep us in place, and the ones that don't
articles.content:
Last weekend, I started to notice that some of the ‘good’ habits I have been consistent with the past few weeks (and by good, I mean habits that objectively improved my subjective well being, as I was able to track) were beginning to really pay off.

I had more energy, more motivation, and it feeling content and mindful seemed to come naturally. Everything I worked on was interesting (my short fuse for AI mistakes was still there, but maybe less so), and I felt like I didn’t have enough time to do all the things that I wanted to.

​Today, I don’t feel that way. I feel like I don’t want to do much. Last evening I finished work with a feeling of uncertainty: I didn’t know why I was doing what I was doing, or what I should be doing. It felt like I had been wasting time.

These swings are natural and probably relatable. It’s only because I’ve been tracking this recently that I even noticed this drastic change. Because I got to notice it, though, I also got to see some of the causes and some interesting phenomena that relate to habits and feeling good.

Feedback loops

Feedback loops are cycles of actions that repeat with modifications based on the previous loop. For example, I play basketball once and get a little bit better, so I play again for longer, and I get even better, etc., etc. This is a positive feedback loop, because the feedback from doing the original things leads to me doing more of it. Negative feedback loops temper the events or conditions of the loop: for example, I play basketball for a long time, I wake up sore and tired, next time I play less.​

Positive feedback occurs when more of the outcome of the loop leads to more of the inputs and less of the outcome leads to less of the input. Negative loops occur when more of the outcome leads to less of the input, and vice versa.

These loops are constantly taking place within our motivation system. Some that I’ve noticed:

Positive

  • The interplay of sleep and diet. Sleep is somewhat of a wonder drug in terms of the benefits it has when done right. One of those is stronger prefrontal cortex (PFC) control. In other words, willpower. When I sleep well, it’s easy not to eat close to bedtime (because even if I feel the desire to, my PFC is able to decide not to). So ‘sleeping well’ leads to more ‘sleeping well’: a positive feedback loop. It also works in the opposite direction: if I sleep poorly, my nighttime decisions degrade in quality, and I more often find myself eating before bed and getting less quality sleep, degrading my willpower the following day.

  • Feeling energized by habits. When I’m doing these healthy behaviors, I tend to have more energy and a more positive outlook. That makes doing them easier. The same goes the other way–if I don’t feel good, it’s hard to start doing behaviors that are good for me.

These loops can be extremely beneficial or very detrimental. When they are spiraling in the wrong direction, it’s really hard to turn them around. At the same time, when they’re going in the right direction, it seems easy and effortless to continue them in that way.

One of the most common fallacies about feeling good is that the things that make me feel good will always be as difficult to do as when I first begin. The assumption is often enough to destroy whatever small hold the PFC had on the situation, which defaults us to the negative behavior. It completely discounts the power of positive feedback.

Negative

It’s not all parades and cupcakes. There is an interesting feedback loop I discovered that is quite challenging to reckon with–and I believe to be one of the reasons that I’m not feeling 100% like I was last weekend.

  • Excitement and sleep. So this loop starts out like the food one. I sleep well, so I have more energy. I also feel more motivated, and the things I do feel more meaningful. I work hard, and time seems to just fly by. Nighttime comes, and I should probably close the laptop, but I’m still having so much fun, so I let myself continue. More time flies by. Pretty soon, it’s past my bedtime, and I haven’t even eaten dinner. This then leads to me getting less sleep. The upside–tomorrow I’ll have less energy, which in this closed environment will lead to my sleeping earlier. Classic negative loop, doing the thing leads to less of it.

I find this situation to be more profound than the positive feedback loops. It almost feels like a betrayal of the past version of myself that built up these energy reserves, which the present I have leeched off of with no plan to replenish them.​

These things happen, and I think it’s best to be aware of them. If, like me, you also want to feel better, knowing the ways in which you are pushed in that direction or held back from it makes the pursuit more doable. It also makes it more understandable: I don’t have to berate myself for eating a big meal an hour before bed; instead, I can make a plan for tomorrow, knowing my PFC won’t be as strong tomorrow night either. Loops exist, so we might as well use them.

articles.title: Repeated (Un)success
articles.subtitle: The best lessons from past successes require some digging
articles.description: The best lessons from past successes require some digging
articles.content:
Years ago, I felt what I thought to be a revelation around success.

I was struggling with the idea of building a successful business. I had taken enough half-hearted shots at it, and failed each time that I was learning that I couldn’t do it, and never would. On a fundamental level, it felt like something I was not capable of.

The revelation came when I looked back on other areas of my life, areas where I had found success, despite having previously doubted that I would achieve it. The easiest one that I will use as the example today is fitness. Getting fit seems to be the canonical pursuit of self-improvement, and it’s easy and fits in a nice box.

As a teenager, I went through several phases of both running and weightlifting. No consistent routine ever stuck, and because of that, I never noticed any significant changes from my efforts. I began to ‘learn’ that I would never be able to stick with a routine that got me the results I wanted.

Then, I did. Soon after going to college, I built a gym routine, and it’s stayed with me since (though admittedly it’s gone through many phases and adaptations along the way).

My idea with business was basically: found the belief that you can build a successful business in the fact that you have had success in these other areas, despite not believing at the time that you could. Weirdly, I was trying to build belief out of past disbelief.

And that revelation, 2 years later, has led me to….
…still no successful business.

Today, I want to offer an addendum to my former revelation, and add-on that I believe will be key to finding success in an area of life where success has come from before.

This add-on avoids rooting in hand-wavy ideas like “self-belief” and instead bases its hypothesis on objective reasoning.

The following is my 3-step process to begin finding success in any area:

  1. Acknowledge the areas of life where you formerly felt unsuccessful, and now feel successful in. Stretch the limits here. It could be fitness, business, career, academics, athletics, relationships, communication skills, or anything you can think of. Something you improved, despite the fact that at some point, you didn’t believe you could.

  2. Identify the things that changed in each area when you began to find success.

  3. Determine how those “things that changed” can apply to this new area.

When I reflect on the fitness routine that “stuck”, there were a few key components

  • My environment was fresh for new routines. I had started college in a new city, and it was my first time living on my own. There were none of the cues that I had associated with my former routine.

  • I met someone else who was motivated and also starting at square one.

  • I lived close to a gym (as most college students living on campus do). There was little friction.

  • I saw progress in a few weeks. This wasn’t to say I was satisfied, but I saw that it was possible.

Those elements can easily be applied to my journey with entrepreneurship. Each of them clearly has takeaways that are universal, not just specific to the fitness realm. And most importantly, this isn’t advice given by a book, a podcast, or instagram reel. It’s coming from me, from something that actually worked for me in the past.

articles.title: Leaning Back
articles.subtitle: "I" am not as important as I think
articles.description: "I" am not as important as I think
articles.content:
I’ve been working on-edge lately. “3 cups of coffee” has become a semi-regular occurrence, depending on how stressed out I want to get about the work I’m doing. For whatever reason, I’m drawn to the anxiously urgent style of work I do when too much caffeine is coursing through my veins.

It feels like “I” am on the edge of my face, like my consciousness itself is trying to burst out and just get done what needs to be done in front of me. What that actually looks like is a short temper for work items - anytime my computer loads longer than it should, or an AI helper of mine makes a mistake, I feel my blood simmer (not usually to a full boil, but sometimes).

As I said, there are times when I’m drawn to that on-edge style of being. It feels productive. At the same time, it’s stressful, and there must be a different way. I’m going to explore that other way.

I’m going to split up these two ways of being by the subjective feeling of where my consciousness exists.

It is abstract, as all talk around consciousness is, but I think it is useful in splitting the two states.

In the first, which I already described, I feel like my consciousness is leaning forward.

The other option is for my consciousness to lean back.

Take a second to feel that out. You may be able to discern the two states as you’re reading this–look intensely into the page, notice the “you” you identify with begin to move into your eyes. Notice the feeling of effort. In this state, it feels like you’re really trying to read and understand this.

Now, lean back. Imagine your inner homunculus leaning against the back of the inside of your skull. Feel your eyes relax a little. Notice that you are still reading this (and understanding it), but it doesn’t feel so much like trying.

Another cue to experience this is to imagine your visual field as a movie screen. Take in everything you see right now, but imagine taking a step back and noticing that this is all being shown to you, but it is not you. That separation is what goes away when I have too much caffeine.

The profound takeaway here is that my brain and body still function fine when my consciousness leans back. I often assume that I am the driver, and without “me” feeling like I’m right there, putting in effort, nothing would get done. It makes many things seem harder.

Imagine going for a run in this state, where you are just a bystander to your experience. Your body knows how to run; it knows where to go. You just think it has to be hard, but it doesn’t–not to “you” at least.

Or working. Some types of work seem to aid more in this style of being, especially creative work. For whatever reason, strict processes and technical work seem to pull me forward in my head. But writing, playing the piano, and <fill in your creative activity of choice> happen more easily this way. There is no resistance. It just happens, and I get to sit idly by while it does.​

It allows for what feels to be a stream-of-consciousness expression, where the me who is always trying is taken out of the picture, and thoughts that are always there are allowed to make their way out. It sounds like that would be trash (I recognize that I may be digging myself into a hole here), but it doesn’t seem that it always is.​

How would your life change if you didn’t always need to be trying so hard?

You could just let yourself do the things you know how to do, the things you are good at, without you getting in the way. We are built for it. There’s no need to constantly be on edge.

What would happen if you leaned back?
